provider_responses.text:
Yes, you normally need money for both the school and living costs.

For a student residence permit, UDI usually requires proof that you can support yourself for the study period. Based on the figure discussed:

- **12,000 NOK/month**
- **12 months:** about **144,000 NOK**
- In euros, roughly **€12,000–€13,000**, depending on exchange rate.

But the real amount can differ depending on what you choose:

- **Folk high school:** tuition often includes accommodation and meals, so the school can document part of your living costs.
- **Private language school:** you usually pay tuition separately and still need money for rent, food, transport, etc.
- **University:** public tuition may be lower for some students, but living-funds proof is still required; non-EU/EEA students may also have tuition fees.

You generally need to show the funds through a bank statement, money deposited to a Norwegian school’s account, scholarship documentation, or other accepted financial proof.

provider_responses.text:
The most important point is this:

**It is not enough to have 12,000 NOK available each month after you arrive. You normally need to prove the money in advance when applying for permission to stay as a student.**

For a one-year course, that means you may need to show roughly:

- **144,000 NOK for living costs** for 12 months  
- **Plus school tuition/fees**, if they are not already paid  
- **Plus travel, insurance, visa/application fees, and possibly a housing deposit**

So your real starting budget can be much higher than 144,000 NOK.

For example:

| Cost | Typical amount |
|---|---:|
| Living-funds proof for 12 months | ~144,000 NOK |
| Housing deposit | 20,000–50,000 NOK |
| First month’s rent | 7,000–15,000 NOK |
| School/language-course fee | varies greatly |
| Flight, insurance, initial costs | several thousand NOK |

A folk high school can sometimes be easier financially because accommodation and meals may be included in the school price. In that case, the school’s confirmation can help show that some of your living expenses are already covered. But you still need enough money for personal expenses and any amount UDI requires.

Also, do **not** assume you can arrive in Norway as a visitor and then rely on finding work to meet the requirement. For a student-based stay, the financial proof must usually be ready **before** approval. A future job offer or “I will find work” is generally not the same as documented funds.

provider_responses.text:
Another important aspect is that **the type of school/course must actually qualify you for a student residence permit**.

Not every course that calls itself a “school,” “college,” or “language programme” will let you legally stay in Norway beyond a normal visitor stay.

Before paying anything, confirm all of these points in writing:

1. **The programme is full-time**  
   A part-time language class or occasional course is usually not enough.

2. **The school is recognised/eligible for a student residence permit**  
   Ask the school directly:  
   *“Can this programme be used as the basis for a Norwegian student residence permit, and do you issue the required admission confirmation for UDI?”*

3. **The course lasts long enough**  
   Very short courses may not support a residence permit. The exact requirement depends on the permit route and your nationality.

4. **You receive a formal admission letter**  
   It should state:
   - your full name;
   - course name;
   - start and end dates;
   - full-time study status;
   - tuition amount and whether it is paid;
   - whether accommodation/meals are included.

5. **The school can document payments and accommodation**  
   If you pay tuition, housing, or meals through the school, obtain official receipts. These can matter when showing how your living costs are covered.

6. **Do not pay large fees until you know the refund policy**  
   If your residence permit is refused, you need to know whether the school refunds tuition, housing payments, or deposits. Get this policy in writing before sending money.

The practical risk is paying a private school thousands of NOK, arriving or applying based on its course, and later discovering that the course does not meet the immigration requirements. The school’s promise alone is not enough—make sure its documentation matches what UDI requires.

provider_responses.text:
Here is a practical way to handle this before paying any school.

## Step 1: Choose only a full-time programme

Ask the school:

> “Is this a full-time programme, how many teaching hours per week does it have, and can it be used for a Norwegian student residence permit?”

Avoid relying on:
- evening classes;
- part-time Norwegian courses;
- online-only programmes;
- short tourist-style courses;
- individual university courses without a degree-study admission.

## Step 2: Ask for these documents before payment

Request a written offer/admission letter showing:

- your full legal name and date of birth;
- school name and address;
- programme name;
- exact start and end date;
- confirmation that it is full-time;
- total tuition fee;
- amount already paid and amount remaining;
- whether housing, food, insurance, or transport is included;
- the school’s refund policy if your residence permit is refused.

If they will not provide this in writing, do not pay.

## Step 3: Calculate the real amount you need

Use this formula:

**School cost + UDI living-funds amount + housing deposit + first month’s rent + travel/insurance = minimum money needed**

Example for a language school:

| Item | Example |
|---|---:|
| One-year full-time language programme | 45,000 NOK |
| Living funds for 12 months | 144,000 NOK |
| Deposit + first rent | 30,000 NOK |
| Flight, insurance, basic setup | 10,000 NOK |
| **Estimated total needed** | **229,000 NOK** |

Example for a folk high school where accommodation and meals are included:

| Item | Example |
|---|---:|
| School year including room and meals | 140,000 NOK |
| Personal spending / required additional funds | depends on documentation |
| Flight, insurance, clothes, phone, etc. | 10,000–20,000 NOK |
| **Estimated total** | often around **150,000–180,000+ NOK** |

These are planning examples, not guaranteed UDI figures. The exact required amount and what can be deducted for paid accommodation/meals must be checked for your application.

## Step 4: Check whether you need to apply before travelling

This depends heavily on your nationality.

- If you are from outside the EU/EEA, you will commonly need a **student residence permit before moving to Norway**.
- You should not plan to enter as a visitor and simply remain after the 90-day visitor period.
- If you are an EU/EEA citizen, the process is different: you may have registration rights, but you still need genuine study status and enough money to support yourself.

## Step 5: Send this exact message to every school

> Hello. I am an international applicant and need to know whether your programme can support a Norwegian student residence permit.  
>   
> Please confirm in writing:  
> 1. Whether the programme is full-time;  
> 2. The weekly teaching hours;  
> 3. The course start and end dates;  
> 4. Whether you issue an official admission letter for a UDI student-residence application;  
> 5. Tuition and all additional fees;  
> 6. Whether accommodation and meals are included;  
> 7. Your refund policy if my residence permit is refused.  
>   
> Thank you.

## Bottom line

Do not choose a school just because it accepts you quickly. Choose it only if it gives you formal documents, is suitable for the residence-permit route available to you, and you can prove the full amount of money required before you apply.

provider_responses.text:
A major thing that may be misunderstood is the difference between:

1. **being accepted by a school**, and  
2. **being granted legal permission to live in Norway.**

They are separate decisions.

A school may accept you and take payment, but UDI can still refuse a student residence permit if the programme, finances, documents, or your situation do not meet the requirements. Never treat school admission as a guarantee of permission to stay.

Other common issues to watch for:

- **Nationality matters.** EU/EEA/Swiss citizens and non-EU/EEA citizens have different entry, registration, and residence rules. The correct route cannot be confirmed without knowing your passport nationality.

- **“Recognised school” is not automatically enough.** A legitimate school can offer a real course, while that particular course still does not satisfy the requirements for a residence permit.

- **A language course is not always a student-permit route.** Do not assume a private Norwegian-language course qualifies merely because it is full-time or expensive. Get confirmation from the relevant immigration authority and the school’s written documentation.

- **Course timing matters.** Even if a school has rolling admission, the permit application and processing may take time. “Start now” may be impossible in practice if you need approval before travel.

- **The funds must be accessible.** Borrowed money temporarily placed in an account, unclear cash deposits, or money held by someone else may cause problems. You need clear evidence that you genuinely control the funds and can use them for your stay.

- **Tuition and living funds are different.** Paying school fees does not automatically prove you have enough for rent, food, and daily expenses—unless the relevant costs are formally included and documented.

- **Housing can be difficult.** A school may admit you without offering accommodation. Renting privately often requires a deposit, proof of income or funds, and sometimes a Norwegian bank account or guarantor.

- **Work is not a safe financial plan.** Student work rights, if available, are limited and depend on the permit. Employment may be hard to find, especially without Norwegian language skills. You should be able to meet the financial requirement without expecting work income.

- **Refund risk is real.** Check whether the school refunds tuition, room fees, and deposits if the immigration application is rejected or delayed. Some fees can be non-refundable.

The safest next step is to identify your nationality, intended arrival date, and total available budget. Then verify the exact immigration route before paying any school.

- **Refund risk is real.** Check whether the school refunds tuition, room fees, and deposits if the immigration application is rejected or delayed. Some fees can be non-refundable.

The safest next step is to identify your nationality, intended arrival date, and total available budget. Then verify the exact immigration route before paying any school.

Before you pay any school, do these 3 things:

1. **Check your immigration route based on your nationality.**  
   EU/EEA and non-EU/EEA citizens have different rules.

2. **Get written proof from the school** that the exact programme is:
   - full-time;
   - eligible for a student residence application;
   - supported by an official admission letter;
   - clear about tuition, housing/meals, and refunds if your permit is refused.

3. **Make sure you have the full money upfront.**  
   Plan for living funds, tuition, housing deposit, first rent, travel, and insurance—not just 12,000 NOK per month.

Do not rely on finding work after arrival, and do not assume school admission automatically gives you the right to stay.
